You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC observations

## Task task-28d3df76 — connect/extend aligned marker strokes (rule unresolved)
This task appeared with different palette and dimensions across three demos (marker colors 5, 8, 9; backgrounds 6, 1, 0) and a test (marker 2 on background 7). The demos introduce color 3 in stretches/regions while retaining marker cells. The exact transformation was not solved: all 8 test submissions were incorrect. Do **not** rely on the older claim that simple filling between consecutive aligned marker cells was confirmed; that claim was wrong.

### Demonstration 3 (clearest evidence)
Input 7x17, background 0, markers 9 at (row 1, col 1), (1,15), (2,14), (5,9). Output is identical except cells (1,2) through (1,14) become 3. Thus the pair of same-row markers at row 1 is joined by a horizontal 3 stroke; other unaligned marker(s) remain unchanged. This is strong evidence for drawing a line between aligned marker pairs, but does not establish how to choose pairs when many markers share a row/column, nor whether perpendicular connections are also drawn.

### Demonstration 2 (20x14, marker 8/background 1)
Output adds color 3 in many places, including long horizontal and vertical-looking strokes/regions; marker 8 cells remain 8. There are also some output 1 cells apparently associated with larger areas/regions, so simple “replace all cells between every consecutive aligned pair by 3” is not an adequate explanation without further geometry. Preserve this ambiguity for future recurrence; request demos strategically before submitting.

### Demonstration 1 (20x30, marker 5/background 6)
Output similarly introduces 3 (and some 6) amid the scattered 5s. Marker 5s appear retained. Large areas/background transformed in a structured way; a naive convex-hull or bounding-box theory was considered but never verified.

### Test grid for this instance
10x19, background 7, markers 2 at rows (0:c14), (1:c0,c2,c4,c6,c8,c10,c13,c15,c17), (2:c9,c16), (3:c0,c8,c16), (4:c4,c8), (5:c15), (6:c4,c6,c11,c13), (7:c7,c16), (8:c2,c6,c13,c15), (9:c7). All eight proposed outputs were wrong. Several attempts variously filled horizontal and vertical spans, and one used only horizontal spans; thus none of those naïve variants is validated. The task likely has a richer line/ray/region rule or selective pairing; use the demo outputs for careful coordinate-level reconstruction if this pattern recurs.

General transferable evidence: these ARC tasks may encode sparse points that are connected/aligned with color 3, with marker points preserved; palette and canvas size can vary. Demo 3 proves at least one horizontal aligned pair is joined inclusively between its endpoints (endpoints themselves kept as 9).
